newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - UBS sees 1997 Latam GDP exceeding 4 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UBS sees 1997 Latam GDP exceeding 4 pct.

text.p: A moderate 1997 economic growth rate of just over 4.0 percent is expected to curb price pressures in some Latin American countries where inflation is still running in double and triple digits, UBS Securities said.

Revising its 1996 gross domestic product (GDP) forecast to 3.4 percent growth from 2.9 percent, UBS said several Latin markets had experienced "a stronger-than-expected recovery in industrial output."
A benign external environment and temperate economic developments will allow the market "to hold on to its gains so far this year," UBS said in its quarterly forecast report.
UBS said those developments will set the pace for further contraction in yield spreads though the narrowing will be at a much slower pace than in 1996.
Specifically, Mexican Brady bonds will maintain their status as being the most expensive in the market "but will find it hard to outperform," UBS said, which is recommending a market weighting.
Mexico's economic recovery has remained on course, according to the report. But growth, which has been fueled by strong export demand, is likely to wane next year.
"In the absence of strong domestic demand we expect (Mexico's) growth to slow in 1997 to just over 4 percent," it said.
Colombian eurobonds, which were among the worst performers in Latin America in 1996, should show some "modest outperformance over the coming months," UBS said.
Argentina's recent political and economic problems have faded while economic recovery has taken a firm hold, the report said.

"With the economy growing close to five percent in 1997 the fiscal problems will ease, but the trade position will deteriorate and we expect the current account deficit will widen to over $5.0 billion," it said.

"The market will probably take this in stride but will become increasingly concerned over the large amount of new issuance needed to cover 1997 amortizations," UBS said, adding that there was a risk that Argentine Bradys will lag during the next quarter as investors focus on that trend.
Brazil's anti-inflation policy is likely to continue, UBS said. "The policy has been successful in reducing inflation, and we expect to see it in single digits next year," it said.
UBS expects Brazil's Bradys to remain fair value at current levels but "could outperform on news or even rumors of further buybacks."
Venezuela's growing confidence in the domestic market, the debt buyback program and continued capital inflows suggest a robust performance by that country's Brady bonds, it said.
Venezuela's economic activity in the non-oil sector may be the best since 1993, UBS economists said.
